sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
sections.body_md:
An exact line search minimizes the objective along a ray. Many iterations only need a step that decreases the objective enough. The Armijo test makes that idea numeric. Fix a parameter \(c\) strictly between zero and one, and accept a trial length \(t > 0\) when the new value sits at or below the current value plus \(c\) times \(t\) times the directional derivative.

Because the directional derivative of a descent direction is negative, the right-hand side is smaller than the current value. It is also larger than the pure tangent prediction, since \(c < 1\) and the slope is negative: the comparison line falls more slowly than the tangent. The first-order expansion says the function tracks the tangent for a short step, so it starts out below the shallower comparison line. A sufficiently small trial is therefore accepted. No Hessian is required for that argument.

Backtracking uses the fact. Start at a trial length \(t_0\). If the inequality fails, replace the trial by \(\beta t\) with a fixed factor \(\beta\) strictly between zero and one, and test again. The trials shrink geometrically, and the first-order argument says the loop cannot reject every one of them.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The accepted step satisfies
\[
f(x + t d) \le f(x) + c\, t\, \nabla f(x)^T d, \qquad 0 < c < 1.
\]
A rejected trial is replaced by \(\beta t\) with \(0 < \beta < 1\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(f(u) = u^2\) at \(u = 5\), so the value is \(25\) and the derivative is \(10\). Take \(d = -1\), the parameter \(c = 0.1\), and the trial \(t = 6\). The directional derivative is \(-10\). The right-hand side is \(25 + 0.1 \cdot 6 \cdot (-10) = 25 - 6 = 19\). The trial point is \(u = -1\), where the function equals \(1\), and \(1\) is below \(19\).

The latch value is 19. The test accepts this trial. A much longer trial could fail the same test even though the direction descends, because the parabola turns upward. Backtracking would then halve, or otherwise shrink, the trial and test again.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Reversing the inequality accepts steps that have not fallen far enough and rejects steps that have fallen further. The test is an upper bound on the new value. A second slip is to set \(c\) bigger than one. The comparison line would then drop faster than the tangent, and a smooth function with a nonzero second derivative will fail the test for every small step. A third is to multiply a rejected trial by a factor bigger than one. That lengthens the step and walks away from the short-step regime that the proof uses. A fourth is to treat a passing trial as the exact minimizer along the line. Armijo only claims sufficient decrease.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: When the direction is the negative gradient and the gradient is Lipschitz with constant \(L\), every step shorter than \(2(1 - c)/L\) is guaranteed to pass Armijo. That link is the sufficient-decrease lemma. The same backtracking loop damps a Newton direction: the direction stays the Newton step, and the length shrinks until the inequality holds. Adding a curvature condition on top of Armijo produces the Wolfe pair of tests, which quasi-Newton updates use to keep a positive definite approximation.
